big: A toothpaste maker raises prices slightly and sales barely change. A telecom start-up needs licences and huge spending just to begin. Profit goes to companies that rivals cannot easily copy.

lines: Porter's five forces: rivals, new entrants, substitutes, buyers and suppliers. Barriers to entry keep new firms out. An economic moat is a lasting advantage, such as a loved brand. Pricing power is raising prices without losing many customers.

rows: how easily can new firms join?
how much power do they hold?

q: An analyst checks how easily new firms can enter and how much power customers hold. Which framework is this?
why: It judges competition through five forces. That matches the case described.
Sum of the parts is a valuation method. That does not match this case.
A DCF is a valuation method. That does not match this case.
A moving average is a chart tool. It does not fit the facts given.

q: A telecom start-up needs licences and huge spending on airwaves. What are these?
why: Pricing power is about raising prices.
They make it hard for new firms to join.
A discount rate is a valuation input.

q: A well-loved brand keeps customers even when cheaper options appear. What is this?
why: A valuation trap is cheap for a reason. It does not fit the facts given.
A lasting advantage that protects profits. That matches the case described.
A breakout is a chart move. It does not answer what was asked.
A capital call is an AIF demand. The details here point elsewhere.

q: A toothpaste maker raises prices slightly and sales barely change. What does it have?
why: A margin call is a futures demand. It does not fit the facts given.
Penetration is about usage. It does not answer what was asked.
A hurdle rate is a return threshold. The details here point elsewhere.
It can raise prices without losing many customers.

pts: Porter's five forces: rivals, entrants, substitutes, buyers, suppliers.
Barriers to entry and a moat protect profits.
Pricing power: raising prices without losing customers.
